qa.q: What could Ritu and Madhuri do to make sure it is handled safely, and why?

In the small town of Harda, everyone took the same bus to the Government Higher Secondary School. For five months, Wasim sat alone at the back while two older boys flicked his ears and called him "buffalo". He told no one. He thought if he stayed quiet, they would get bored.

They didn't. His marks slipped. He stopped raising his hand in class. In the mornings he started saying his stomach hurt.

His elder sister Swati noticed he left for the bus later and later. One Monday she found him hiding behind the flour mill instead of at the bus stop, eyes red.

She sat down on the step beside him. He told her everything. Swati walked him to school herself, straight to his class teacher, Mr. Tiwari, who listened, told Wasim it wasn't his fault, and called the principal and their parents that afternoon.

qa.q: Where did Swati find Wasim that Monday?
qa.a: She found him hiding behind the flour mill instead of at the bus stop.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling during the months he stayed silent?
qa.a: He hoped the boys would get bored, but he felt scared and increasingly low, which shows in his slipping marks and stomach aches.

qa.q: What might have helped Wasim much earlier?
qa.a: Telling Swati, a parent or a teacher in the first week, so an adult could act before months of teasing wore down his confidence.

qa.q: How might Swati have felt finding Wasim behind the flour mill?
qa.a: Swati was probably shocked and protective, which is why she walked him straight to his teacher instead of waiting.

grounding: Shows a student enduring bullying silently for months, losing confidence and avoiding school, until a sibling notices and a teacher acts the same day.

Wei's family had moved to Nairobi when his mother took a hospital job, and from his first week at the international school, three boys made jokes about his eyes whenever he walked past. Wei said nothing. He smiled, looked at the floor, and hoped they'd find someone else.

By March, four months in, he'd stopped going to the canteen. He ate in the library, then in the toilets. He started asking to stay home with headaches.

His classmate Abebe had seen it all and had been quiet too. One afternoon he found Wei sitting on the stairs behind the gym during a lesson, just staring.

"This isn't okay," Abebe said. "Come with me." They went together to the head of year, Ms. Wanjiru. She listened to both of them, told Wei none of it was his fault, and phoned his mother before the last bell to arrange a meeting for the next morning.

qa.q: Where did Wei start eating after he stopped going to the canteen?
qa.a: He ate in the library, then in the toilets.

qa.q: What does Wei's smiling and looking at the floor suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt hurt and afraid, hoping that by staying quiet he could avoid making the teasing worse.

qa.q: What else could Abebe have done earlier?
qa.a: Abebe could have sat with Wei at lunch and told a teacher in the first weeks, so Wei did not spend months alone.

qa.q: How might Wei's mother feel getting the phone call?
qa.a: She would likely feel upset and worried, but also grateful the school acted quickly and set a meeting for the next morning.

grounding: Shows a student ignoring racist teasing for months until confidence drops and school feels unbearable, before a classmate brings him to a teacher who acts the same day.
